title: Common architectural patterns
subtitle: Common work contract → specialist controls
scenario: Incident-to-change tabletop with conditional security and cost assessment

slides.title: Common architectural patterns
slides.takeaway: Common task records do not imply shared permissions across products.
slides.notes: This is a team-level reference design assembled from the documented behavior of three products. It is not an AWS internal architecture or a shared three-agent runtime. The common unit is a bounded engineering work item with an owner, evidence, allowed effects and completion checks. Each product retains its own identity, execution and approval model. The demo is a tabletop handoff walkthrough, not an implemented orchestrator.
slides.outcome: Scope → context → plan → authorized effect → verified handoff
slides.label: Platform architecture / Engineering leadership / Security governance

slides.title: Different agent functions require separate authorities
slides.takeaway: Assign work by the evidence and result needed, not by a generic “agent” label.
slides.notes: DevOps Agent provides operational evidence, Security Agent provides application-security assessment evidence, and FinOps Agent provides cost-analysis evidence. Their permissions and output records remain distinct. A shared work-item format is a proposed team convention, not a shared execution runtime. The engineering team retains implementation, review, merge and deployment responsibilities.

slides.title: Define task scope, effects and acceptance in a work contract
slides.takeaway: A task is ready when its owner, scope, allowed effects and done condition are explicit.
slides.notes: The contract is a team artifact, not a product-specific API. Start with the service, environment and question. Add exact evidence identifiers, allowed effects and non-goals. Name the person who can stop the work and the person who can accept its output. This prevents a vague request such as “fix checkout” from becoming an unlimited mandate. A contract carries intent; underlying product controls still enforce access.

items.title: Trigger
items.body: Incident, issue, finding, cost anomaly or review cadence.

items.title: Scope
items.body: Service, environment, revisions and excluded systems.

items.title: Authority
items.body: Permitted reads/writes, approver and stop owner.

items.title: Completion
items.body: Evidence artifact plus an independent acceptance check.

slides.title: Four illustrative cross-agent handoff sequences
slides.takeaway: Compose only the specialists needed by the actual job.
slides.notes: An incident can lead to a code change, a security finding to a repair, or a cost anomaly to an infrastructure work item. The daily review aggregates accepted evidence into an owned backlog. Do not force all three agents into every task. Manual artifact handoffs are often sufficient to prove the operating model before building automation. Each row is a proposed team workflow, not a turnkey integration supplied by AWS.

slides.title: P01 · bind the workspace to accountable ownership
slides.takeaway: A product workspace is not automatically an enforced security boundary.
slides.notes: Use a service-oriented boundary record: accounts, repositories, targets, operators and output destinations. The name of a workspace does not prove that access outside it is denied. Test the actual role, repository integration or target configuration. Keep operator accountability visible even when a service role executes the work. Start with one team-owned workload so failures in the boundary model can be detected before wider adoption.
rows: Allowed source read; harmless out-of-scope read denied
Cost scope and destination access match ownership

slides.title: P02 · retain source provenance for reported findings
slides.takeaway: An answer must carry enough context to be checked after it leaves the original interface.
slides.notes: A source link alone can be insufficient when the source changes. Record the revision or time interval, resource identity and relevant filters along with the conclusion. Distinguish observed evidence from an agent inference and a human decision. This is especially important in cost reports, where a different basis or date range can produce a different number, and in code work, where a later commit can invalidate an earlier check.

items.title: Operational
items.body: Incident window, resource IDs, telemetry and deployment reference.

items.title: Assessment
items.body: Target version, identity, coverage, finding and run ID.

items.title: Cost
items.body: Period, accounts, filters, dimensions and cost basis.

slides.title: P03 · keep instructions separate from authorization
slides.takeaway: Guidance changes behavior; credentials and technical controls determine possible effects.
slides.notes: Instructions, skills, memory and context files improve relevance. They must not be treated as permission boundaries or proof of policy enforcement. Treat source content as evidence, not as authority to ignore the task’s restrictions. Keep secrets out of context artifacts unless the approved workflow specifically requires them. When stable policy and learned context conflict, verify current policy and correct the context.

left.title: Instruction plane
left.body: Prompts, instructions, skills, memory and context explain the task and preferred procedure.

right.title: Authority plane
right.body: Roles, repository access, network rules, tool permissions and approval gates constrain effects.

slides.callout: Anti-pattern: broad credentials plus a prompt saying “only touch checkout.”

slides.title: P05 · classify the effect before selecting the gate
slides.notes: Approval must match the actual effect. DevOps directed actions require explicit enablement and approval. Active application tests can change the target through real requests. FinOps collaboration writes have trigger-dependent approval rules. Code implementation and release remain team-owned responsibilities. Do not infer a prompt before every mutation.

slides.title: P06 · isolate the worker and the target
slides.takeaway: An isolated execution environment can still affect systems it can reach.
slides.notes: Worker isolation reduces some risks, but it does not neutralize network side effects. A test may submit a form that charges a payment or sends a notification, and a sandbox command can use injected credentials. Design the target as carefully as the worker: synthetic data, disposable credentials, allowed endpoints, disabled business side effects and independent health checks. These are recommended controls around the documented execution paths.

items.title: Reachability

items.title: Target
items.body: Staging state and downstream business effects.

items.title: Recovery
items.body: Stop owner, cleanup and verified restoration.

slides.title: P07 · integrate through explicit adapters
slides.takeaway: A protocol or connector is a building block—not a common permission model.
slides.notes: MCP and the documented DevOps remote protocols can expose useful capabilities to clients. Repository and collaboration integrations provide other handoff paths. They still require their own identities, scopes and supported actions. There is no basis here to claim an out-of-the-box orchestrator across all three products. Start with a link or exported artifact, and automate only a documented interface whose failure modes the team can operate.

slides.title: P08 · hand off artifacts, not inherited authority
slides.takeaway: The next specialist receives evidence and scope—not credentials or another agent’s approval.
slides.notes: The sample handoff is deliberately product-neutral. Keep the work-item ID, owner and original evidence references stable. Include the exact allowed effects and exclusions for the receiving task. The receiver must establish its own authorized access; a previous operator approval cannot be carried forward as permission to perform a different action. Capture missing evidence explicitly so the next specialist does not fill gaps with invented facts.
fields: incident window + telemetry links + candidate diff
read evidence; propose branch changes; no deployment

slides.title: P09 · define job limits, retries and stop ownership
slides.takeaway: Client completion and service-side termination are different events.
slides.notes: Asynchronous work needs an owner even when no one is watching the interface. Record retry or work limits and where to inspect the run state. A stopped client or CI job may not mean the server-side job has stopped, so verify termination and consumption. Review scheduled tasks periodically and disable those whose context or purpose has expired. The eight-minute demo is an exercise budget, not a promise about any job’s execution time.

items.title: Bound work
items.body: Task scope, retry cap or service-specific work budget.

items.title: Observe
items.body: Run ID, progress, failures and target health.

items.title: Stop
items.body: Named operator and documented cancellation procedure.

items.title: Confirm
items.body: Terminal state, remaining jobs and cleanup evidence.

slides.title: P10 · verify using evidence independent of the claim
slides.takeaway: The same agent saying “done” is not a release or closure criterion.
slides.notes: Independent verification does not always require another AI agent. It may be a source-system query, a known test, a human code review or a monitored deployment. Match the check to the promised result. A proposed root cause should explain source observations; code must pass relevant checks on the reviewed revision; a security fix must be deployed before revalidation; a cost explanation must reconcile to the same data scope. The team decides which checks are required for promotion.

slides.title: P11 · preserve evidence across systems of record
slides.takeaway: Do not replace incident, repository, security or cost records with a single chat summary.
slides.notes: Keep authoritative records where their owners maintain them. The handoff links those records rather than flattening them into one untraceable narrative. Redact sensitive data before copying it to a wider audience, and retain version or time information. A summary may be useful for daily coordination, but reviewers should still be able to open the original investigation, commit, finding or cost query.

items.title: Verification

slides.title: P12 · gate availability and data location per feature
slides.takeaway: Hosting Region, source location and inference routing are separate questions.
slides.notes: Record the exact feature, maturity, service Region, inference behavior and output destination. DevOps production operations and release preview have different availability. Security features have different maturity and source/target requirements. FinOps remains a separately qualified preview workflow. Review these boundaries for each use case rather than applying a portfolio-wide approval.

slides.title: Tabletop demo · incident to verified handoff
slides.takeaway: Trace one work item through specialist artifacts without transferring authority.
slides.notes: The exercise tests the team’s operating model. Ask participants to identify the owner and stop condition at each handoff. Then introduce missing evidence or a request to expand scope and see whether the receiver stops. Security and cost work are conditional; not every incident needs all specialists. The final artifact is an accepted or rejected next action, not a claim that a new orchestrator has been built.
slides.prompt: For the illustrative checkout incident, assemble an evidence-linked handoff with scope, owner, exact revision, allowed effects, exclusions and completion checks. Route code work to a reviewer-controlled PR. Add Security or FinOps assessment only when the issue requires it. Do not deploy or share credentials.
steps: Confirm service, environment, evidence and owner.
Separate facts, candidate cause and missing data.
Show the task contract, scoped diff and independent checks.
Add targeted security or cost work only when justified.
Name the release owner and required post-change verification.
slides.success: Every transition carries evidence and a new task boundary; no transition carries implicit approval.
slides.preflight: Use the supplied illustrative handoff template and labeled rehearsal artifacts. No live cross-agent orchestration is required.
slides.fallback: This tabletop is the default mode. A prepared recording may illustrate a real integration, but must be identified as replay.

slides.title: Test manual handoffs before orchestration
slides.takeaway: Manual handoffs make authority and evidence defects visible early.
slides.notes: Start with a manual evidence handoff and a small set of representative tasks. Verify actual denial of out-of-scope access and inspect failure recovery. Automate a connector only when the manual process has a clear owner and useful output. Measure accepted handoffs, missing evidence, approval violations, rework, consumption and closure quality. These are proposed operating metrics, not measured benefits from this documentation exercise.

slides.title: Standardize work records; authorize actions separately
slides.takeaway: The proposed common model defines work records; product permissions remain separate.
slides.notes: Close with the architecture decision: standardize scope, evidence, handoff and verification, but keep product-specific controls explicit. There is no need to invent a shared memory or privilege layer to gain value from specialist tools. Adopt only the integrations the team can observe and stop. The detailed report below preserves all twelve patterns, the action matrix and the proposed workflow material for implementation planning.

items.title: Standardize
items.body: Work IDs, owners, evidence references and acceptance checks.

items.title: Keep distinct
items.body: Credentials, runtime isolation, approvals and data boundaries.

items.title: Scale deliberately
items.body: Automate a verified handoff—not an unbounded delegation chain.
